title: Three names
passages:
The coast-string tender braked so hard its rear end lifted, tires spitting gravel across the ore stub. Miko dropped out of the cab before the dust settled, transponder unit already yanked and tucked into her coat — same trick Rhea pulled on the med rig, same trick everybody learns once they've watched a board swallow a rig whole. The tender was a blunt-nosed runabout, painted Kettering yellow fading to rust, built to meet the long-haul strings at Bitter Wells junction and haul loaders the last leg to the coast.

She carried a folder, heavy with laminate. Three coast tickets. Three names. No apology in her pockets.

The relay shop smelled of hot grease and cold coffee. Teodoro sat at the board, headset cocked, fingers moving over keys that weren't talking back. Nour leaned against the doorframe, arms crossed, boots planted like she could hold the floor down by wanting to. Rhea crouched beside a workbench, Ivo's respirator open on her knees — mask empty, cartridge port dark. And on the couch — Teodoro's couch, the one with the spring that bit your ass — a man sat forward with his right shoulder strapped tight against his chest, Kettering coveralls gray with dust, jaw scraped raw on one side.

Miko counted. Five people. One strapped shoulder that wasn't Ivo's. Ivo was wheezing at the bench, pale but upright.

She let the folder hit the counter with a slap that made Teodoro flinch.

"Three names," she said. "Three tickets. One tender waiting on the stub with its throat cut." She tapped the laminate. "Which one of you needs to stop being who you are?"

The man on the couch didn't look up. His good hand curled on his knee. "Ballast doesn't get a choice."

"Ballast doesn't breathe," Miko said. "You do. So pick a name."

Rhea didn't answer her. She set the mask on the bench and went through into the back bay.

The med rig sat where she'd dragged it in, nose to the wall, doors open, transponder socket empty as a pulled tooth. She climbed in over the sill, past the tool void, and came back out holding a gray can the size of a coffee tin, sealed in foil with the pull tab still bright.

"A cartridge is the part that takes the carbon back out of a breath," she said, sitting down on the floor in front of Ivo with the mask on her knee. "Pull the tab and it starts working. It works about ninety minutes of pumping, and then it's a paperweight." She thumbed the tab. The can hissed. "This one's factory-sealed. It's the last scrubber that came through this node."

"You're cannibalizing a dead rig in front of a reclaimer's warrant," Nour said.

"He's not going to care about the rig," Rhea said. "He wants the pod."

She pressed the fresh cartridge up into the empty port until the collar clicked home. Ivo's face went into the mask. The little green tally lamp came up and started counting down. His shoulders came down half an inch, which for Ivo was a standing ovation.

"Ninety minutes," Rhea said, to the room, not to him. "Diaphragm does the pumping, rubber disc does the seal, and there is no second cartridge on this node. I checked the shop stock twice." She wiped her hands on her thighs. "So don't round up on his air."

"Nobody's rounding," Nour said.

Miko laughed once, without much in it. "Ninety minutes is a long shift in a relay shop. It's nothing at all down-line."

Ivo lifted two fingers off the blanket. Everyone shut up, which was annoying, because he took his time about it.

"That one," he said. The mask fogged and cleared. "The strapped shoulder. Come here where I don't have to shout."

Marlowe got off the couch and came, careful with the arm. Ivo looked at him for a while, the way you look at a gauge you don't trust.

"A name off a ticket is still weight," he said. "That's all a name is, if nobody signs for it. You ride the string to Bitter Wells, you get off at a coast platform with somebody else's letters on your back, and the first loader who asks who put you on the roster — nobody. Nobody put you on. You're weight that walks." He pulled two breaths. "You just get delivered somewhere with nobody to sign for you."

Marlowe's jaw worked on the scraped side. "Weight doesn't get asked questions."

"Weight doesn't get a bunk either," Ivo said. "It gets a number, and the number gets closed."

The tally lamp ticked down a minute. Teodoro said, quietly, "Fourteen minutes to the countersign," and nobody had an answer for that, so Miko opened the folder on the counter and squared the laminate with two fingers, getting ready to say her piece.

Miko turned the top ticket around so the room could read it.

"The run, then. Out the shop door, left at the fuel shed, six hundred meters of gravel to the ore stub, and you keep the shed between you and the north gate the whole way, because that's where the service rig will be parked with an empty cradle and its work lights on. The tender's already sitting on the stub track. Nobody saw it come in, nobody's going to see it go out, because it hasn't got a transponder to be seen with." She flicked the second ticket over. "Stub track to Bitter Wells junction. Forty minutes, no stops. The coast string comes through at 06:40 and holds loading until 06:52, because loader crews ride that string and a roster will wait on its own people. Down-line at Ferris there's a bunk house with a loader's bunk and somebody else's letters on the door. After Ferris it's four hundred kilometers of being somebody else's problem."

"North gate," Rhea said. "Pell's north gate. He'll be standing there at 06:00 with a second signature and an open channel to this board."

"Which is why we go out the back while he watches the front," Miko said. "It isn't clever. It's early."

Rhea looked at the tally lamp on Ivo's mask, doing its arithmetic. "It's 05:46. Your tender makes the junction at 06:26. The string's gone at 06:52. You want me to spend my brother's air on a plan that clears this node twenty-six minutes after the reclaimer signs."

"I want you to spend it on a plan that clears him at all."

"Then say the rest of it," Nour said, from the doorframe. "You've got a folder with three names in it and you've only sold us a truck."

Miko's mouth went flat. She laid the tickets in a row.

"Yusra Pell, gone off a woman at Bitter Wells who's up a pole on the Ferris span tonight and won't be down before noon. That's the safe one, and safe means the yard clerk calls her bunk at fourteen hundred and finds a stranger asleep in it." Second ticket. "Teodor Sabo. Rostered Bay 2 at Kettering, shift start 22:00, and he never clocked in. So his line's already reading absent on a live board, and absent is the one thing a board doesn't argue with. Nobody's going to come looking for a man who's already missing." She put two fingers on the third and didn't move them. "Sabine Cordy. Bought it off her myself in the Kettering yard at half past nine, two hundred, laminate still warm. She clocked off Bay 4 at 21:47 and she never made another board. That name's already a loose line, which means somebody's office has already opened a claim on it, and a reclaimer doesn't get paid for the pod. He gets paid for the line."

Teodoro took his headset off one ear. "Bay 4 is the band on the pod."

"Bay 4 is the band on the pod," Miko said. "She's the only loader out of that shift I could find who was still walking around loose afterward, and she was walking fast."

"Say what you're actually saying," Rhea said.

"I'm saying she saw the lid go down, or she held it, and either way she ran before the count finished." Miko shrugged. "So the name you want him to wear is the one name on this counter that's already been filed as a discrepancy. Congratulations. He'd be traveling as cargo with a claim on it."

Nour pushed off the doorframe. "That's not a plan, that's a delivery with extra steps."

"It's a delivery," Miko said. "You wanted him gone. This is gone."

Marlowe was looking at the third ticket, at Miko's two fingers on it, and not at anybody else. Outside, gravel popped under something heavy coming up the haul road, and the shop's yard lamp swung, and Teodoro's hand stopped over the keys.

Marlowe didn't flinch at the gravel. He took the third ticket from Miko's fingers, turned it over, and read the name printed in the same block laminate as the other two. *Sabine Cordy. Bay 4. Shift 2. Valid through Ferris.*

"Jacket," Miko said. She was already moving, unzipping a faded loader's jacket from her pack — charcoal with the reflective stripes worn thin at the shoulders. "Coveralls off. Jaw clean. Name twice."

He peeled the Kettering coveralls down to his waist, the left sleeve catching on the strap. Miko caught the fabric and worked it free without pulling the bad shoulder. The undershirt underneath was sweat-dark at the collar. She handed him the jacket. He shrugged into it, left arm first, right arm fed careful through the sleeve by Miko's hand. The fit was close across the chest, loose at the waist. She snapped the top two snaps. Turned the collar up.

"Jaw," she said. Her thumb brushed the scraped side, quick and clinical. "You're not Cordy if you touch it. You're not Cordy if you favor the arm. You're not Cordy if you hesitate on the name."

"Cordy," he said.

"Again."

"Cordy."

"Good." She stepped back. "Walk like you're going to a bunk you've slept in before. Don't look at the gate."

Rhea stood from the bench. The mask's tally lamp read 00:82:17 on Ivo's face. She crossed to the tender's cab, the folder in her hand, and didn't look at the yard lamp swinging on its chain or the service rig's work lights painting the haul road white.

The manifest scanner sat bolted to the tender's dash, a black brick with a slot that ate laminate and spat decisions. Rhea fed the folder in, ticket by ticket. The scanner's read head whined. A green bar crawled across its tiny screen.

*Substitution: S. Cordy → D. Marlowe. Manifest hash: clean. Roster sync: clean. Seal integrity: clean.*

The tender's dash flashed *READY* in block letters that hurt to look at.

Rhea turned. Behind her, the node's plate on the shop wall still glowed its single line, untouched by any scanner or tender or wish: *Designation: ballast.*

The service rig crested the rise. No transponder blink. No ID number on the door. Just work lights and an empty cradle, and the heavy hiss of air brakes locking up at the north gate.

Miko still had her hand out, palm up, waiting on the laminate.

Marlowe looked at it. Then he stepped to the counter and laid the third ticket down with the other two, Sabine Cordy's letters to the ceiling, and squared the edge with one finger like a man leaving a station tidy behind him.

Out on the stub the tender's dash went on throwing READY across the empty cab. It would say that all night. It said whatever it was told.

"I did one shift as dirt," Marlowe said. "Somebody wrote four hundred and twelve kilos on a manifest, and the plate on that wall agreed with him, and the repeater in the box agreed with the plate, and a scanner in a truck agreed with all three, and every one of them was sure. I'm not spending the rest of my life as somebody else's dirt."

"Alive as somebody else's dirt," Miko said.

"A loose line with a claim already open on it. Your words, in this room, ten minutes ago." He turned around, careful with the strapped arm. "His office closes Cordy, it closes me inside her name, and nobody at Ferris ever learns there was a man in there. That isn't gone. That's filed. So, different question. Who at this node has a stamp that puts a living man on a board?"

"Down-line has stamps," Miko said. "Down-line has plenty of things. Clean is clean. It said clean."

"You want to know what clean is worth out here? I've got a pretty good estimate."

Teodoro took the headset all the way off, which for Teodoro was shouting.

"A seal authority is a loader with seal class on their bay credential," he said. "Anybody can close a bay. Only seal class can sign that the seals going out on it are the seals it started with, and the line honors that signature. That's all a stamp is. A person the line agreed to believe." He glanced out at Rhea in the cab and left whatever else he knew about her authority unsaid, which cost him something visible. "There isn't one on this node. There isn't one in this yard. And mechanic's authority only puts a name on the board as crew. Pell's token has that board by the throat until somebody countersigns, and he isn't here to lift it. He's out there adding a second signature to it."

Boots on gravel, then. Unhurried. Whoever they belonged to had all shift.

"How far," Marlowe said.

"Far," Miko said.

"Three hundred kilometers," Nour said.

She hadn't come off the doorframe the whole time and she didn't come off it now.

"There's one stamp on this stretch of line that I know of. It sits at Kettering, Bay 4, on a Shift 2 loader's credential." Her chin came up toward the plate on the wall, still glowing its one line under the shop dust. *Designation: ballast.* "Bay 4. The bay stenciled on that pod. The shift that loaded him."

On Ivo's face the tally lamp read 00:71:40 and kept going.

"That shift ends at oh-six-hundred," Nour said. "Which is eleven minutes. When it ends, that loader clocks off the yard and the stamp goes with them, and the nearest seal class after that is a day down the coast. By then he's four hundred and twelve kilos on a reclaimer's cradle with the lid already swung over and you and me both standing here explaining to a frozen board how we were helping."

Nour hadn't finished. She let the tally lamp tick a few times on Ivo's face, then kept going, because nobody in the shop was going to like where she was headed and she knew it.

"Set the stamp down a second. I want everybody looking at the same board when I say this. You run him — tender, junction, string, Ferris, gone. Good for him. Now look at what this node reads like tomorrow." She folded fingers down one at a time. "A warrant we didn't clear. A pod we didn't hand over. A med rig we dragged in with its transponder cut out of it. That's not a frozen board. Frozen thaws and you forget it. That's a *flagged* board — flagged means every resupply after this one gets read by a man in an office before it rolls, and the cycle after that the roster goes thin, because nobody wants a shift on a node the line's got a claim open against."

"So running him isn't gone," Rhea said from the cab. "It's slow."

"It's a slower way to lose the same winter." Nour didn't raise her voice; she didn't have to. "Two roads keep this node fed. Hand him to Pell at the gate — board clears inside the hour, resupply rolls on schedule, we all eat. Or find a seal and stand him on the board as a living man, which the token can't hold against, and Pell drives home with an empty cradle and a grievance." She looked at Marlowe, and it wasn't unkind, which made it worse. "One of those puts food in this node by dark. I'm not telling you which I want. I'm telling you what the numbers do."

"And the part you're saving for last," Rhea said.

Nour's jaw set. Out on the gravel the boots had gone quiet, or moved off, and nobody looked to see which.

"Somebody at this node has been pulling seals out of the shop locker and sending them down the line to whoever re-cut that pod. Bay stock goes out sealed and comes back needing a lie to cover it, and it's gone on long enough we quit counting." She said it to the whole room and to no one face in particular. "That's not Pell's treason. That's ours. So whichever road you take — hand him over, find the seal — somebody standing in this shop answers for it before the week's out. He's not the only one reading this node. He's just the one holding the token."

Nobody hurried to fill the quiet. Miko squared the three tickets she'd already lost.

Teodoro had the headset back on one ear, and he'd clearly been working Kettering the whole time Nour talked, because Teodoro told you everything before you thought to ask. "Kettering dispatch won't take the direct. So I went around it — night board relay, yard channel, the Bay 4 sub. And they're all *open*, I can hear a forklift, I can hear somebody's radio playing — but the second I say Bay 4, or read the number off that plate, the channel drops to a hold tone and comes back with a header stamped on it." He turned the little screen so they could all see. "Reclaimer's office. Every call tonight that touches that bay routes through his desk first. I can raise Kettering till the shift ends. I just can't say the word without him hearing me say it."

"So we can't ask down-line for the stamp," Rhea said.

"We can ask," Teodoro said. "We'd just be asking him."

The tally lamp on Ivo's mask ticked another minute off, and out at the north gate the service rig sat with its work lights burning and its cradle empty, in no hurry at all.

Rhea came out of the cab with the folder squared in her hand and held it out to Miko, laminate down.

"You'll be wanting this back."

Miko took it and didn't put it away. "The scanner liked me. You heard it. Clean hash, clean roster, clean seal."

"The scanner liked everything." Rhea wiped her palm on her thigh, twice, which was what she did instead of raising her voice. "Go back down the line with me. The plate in that pod said 412 kilos, ballast. The repeater inside the box held that plate's word and said it again, all the way to Kettering — a repeater doesn't know anything, it just keeps the last good reading it was handed and reads it out until somebody cuts it. That's how a box that was cold as a stone got to be 36.4 degrees on Teodoro's screen. Then a scanner in a truck read the folder, and the folder read the plate, and the plate read a man with a stamp and a false weight ticket." She nodded at the stub, where READY kept throwing itself around an empty cab. "Four machines, one opinion. Every one of them agreed and every one of them was wrong, and I signed for the whole stack because the screen was green."

"So don't trust screens," Miko said. "Trust me. I'm standing here."

"You're a person with three names in a folder and a claim already open on one of them." Rhea crossed to the wall. "I'm done helping paper travel."

The node's plate was wired glass with a column of light behind it, two meters of it, and the line read that column to decide whether Anza ate this cycle. Under the shop dust it glowed one line, the way it had glowed since Pell's token went in: *Designation: ballast.* Below that, smaller, her own crew entry from before, and under both, a blinking field the token hadn't thought to lock.

The stylus hung on a coiled cord beside the glass. Rhea seated the tip in the port until it clicked, because a stylus that isn't seated writes nothing and complains about it.

"Mechanic's authority," she said. "I can enter crew. I can enter condition. I can't touch designation while his token's in the port, and he knows that, which is why he left condition alone. A reclaimer doesn't think condition is worth freezing."

She wrote it out in block letters, slow, the way you write when people are watching your handwriting.

*Marlowe, Decklan. Alive. Not weight.*

The glass took it. The light behind the letters came up steady, and under her line a new field opened, patient, the size of a thumbprint: *PENDING COUNTERSIGN.*

"That's a wish on a wall," Nour said.

"It's a condition entry with a name on it," Rhea said. "He's crew, he's breathing, and he's not cargo. The only thing missing is a person the line agreed to believe."

Marlowe stood in the borrowed jacket with his scraped jaw turned toward the light, reading his own name off a wall for the second time in an hour, and this time it was spelled the way he'd said it.

The tally lamp on Ivo's mask said 00:64:02.

And the seal locker chirped.

It was the scheduled ping — every shift change the locker ran its own inventory, counted what was on the racks, and said the number out loud in a flat little voice so nobody had to climb up and look. Everybody in that shop had heard it ten thousand times and nobody had ever once listened.

The counter inside the locker ratcheted. The card in the door slot printed its line.

The locker said the number.

Nour was off the doorframe before it finished. Teodoro turned his whole chair around. Miko stopped with the folder half into her coat.

Nobody said anything, because there was nothing to say about a count that came back that far short of the tally card, and because the locker said it out loud, and everybody in the room had heard it, including the man who wasn't from this node.

Miko's hand went to the latch.
